title: Sharing and Practical Deployment
description: Why safetensors replaced pickle for safety, how to publish a model to the Hub, how to write a real license and model card for your own work, and how Spaces provide lightweight demo deployment.

lessons.title: Safetensors vs. Pickle: Why the Format Matters
lessons.description: Understand why safetensors replaced pickle as the standard way to store model weights.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why safetensors is preferred over Python's pickle format for sharing model weights.

sections.title: ⚠️ Pickle can execute arbitrary code
sections.content: Python's `pickle` format, historically used to save PyTorch weights (`.bin` / `.pt` files), can execute arbitrary code when loaded — a serious security risk if you load a checkpoint from an untrusted source. This isn't a theoretical concern; it's a real supply-chain risk for anyone downloading models from the internet.

sections.title: 🔒 Safetensors: data only, no code execution
sections.content:
The `.safetensors` format stores only tensor data — no executable code path — making it much safer to load from an unverified source, and often faster to load too since it avoids pickle's more general (and slower) deserialization.

```python
from safetensors.torch import save_file, load_file

save_file(model.state_dict(), "model.safetensors")
state_dict = load_file("model.safetensors")
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Loading an untrusted `.bin`/`.pt` checkpoint without checking its source.** This is exactly the risk safetensors exists to remove — prefer safetensors files when available.

**Assuming all older models have a safetensors version.** Some older repos only ship pickle-format weights; check before assuming.

**Ignoring `use_safetensors=True` (or automatic preference) when it's available.** Most Hub tooling now prefers safetensors automatically, but it's worth confirming which format you're actually loading.

questions.question: Why is loading a pickle-format (`.bin`/`.pt`) model checkpoint from an untrusted source a security risk?
options: It isn't a risk at all — pickle files are completely safe
Pickle deserialization can execute arbitrary code, so a malicious checkpoint could run harmful code just by being loaded
Pickle files are always larger, which is the only downside
This risk only applies to image models, not language models
questions.explanation: Pickle's deserialization process can execute code embedded in the file, meaning a malicious actor could craft a checkpoint that runs arbitrary code the moment it's loaded — a real supply-chain risk for downloaded weights.

questions.question: What does the safetensors format specifically avoid that makes it safer than pickle?
options: It avoids storing any tensor data at all
It stores only tensor data with no executable code path, so loading it can't trigger arbitrary code execution
It avoids using any file format standards
It avoids working with PyTorch models
questions.explanation: Safetensors is a data-only format — there's no code execution path involved in loading it, which removes the arbitrary-code-execution risk that comes with pickle-based checkpoint files.

questions.question: What should you do when you're not sure whether a Hub model ships weights in safetensors format?
options: Assume it's always safetensors and never check
Check the repo's files, since some older repos only ship pickle-format weights, and prefer safetensors when both are available
Never use that model regardless of format
Format doesn't matter and can be safely ignored
questions.explanation: Not every repo has migrated to safetensors, so it's worth checking which format is actually available and preferring safetensors for the security and loading-speed benefits when it exists.

questions.question: Why is loading a pickle-format (`.bin`/`.pt`) model checkpoint from an untrusted source a security risk?
options: It isn't a risk at all; pickle files are completely safe
Pickle deserialization can execute arbitrary code, so a malicious checkpoint could run harmful code just by being loaded
Pickle files are always larger, which is the only real downside
This risk only applies to image models, not language models
questions.explanation: Pickle's deserialization process can execute code embedded in the file, meaning a malicious checkpoint could run arbitrary code the moment it's loaded — a real supply-chain risk for downloaded weights.

questions.question: What does the safetensors format specifically avoid that makes it safer than pickle?
options: It avoids storing any tensor data at all
It stores only tensor data with no executable code path, so loading it can't trigger arbitrary code execution
It avoids using any established file format standards
It avoids working with PyTorch models entirely
questions.explanation: Safetensors is a data-only format with no code execution path involved in loading it, which removes the arbitrary-code-execution risk that comes with pickle-based checkpoint files.

questions.question: Besides safety, what other practical advantage does safetensors often have over pickle?
options: It is always slower to load than pickle
It's often faster to load, since it avoids pickle's more general (and slower) deserialization process
It requires significantly more disk space than pickle
It cannot store the same tensor data that pickle can
questions.explanation: Beyond safety, safetensors is often faster to load than pickle since it avoids pickle's more general and slower deserialization process.

questions.question: What should you do when you're unsure whether a Hub model ships weights in safetensors format?
options: Always assume it's safetensors and never check
Check the repo's files, since some older repos only ship pickle-format weights, and prefer safetensors when both are available
Never use that model regardless of the format it uses
Format is irrelevant and can always be safely ignored
questions.explanation: Not every repo has migrated to safetensors, so it's worth checking which format is actually available and preferring safetensors for its security and loading-speed benefits when it exists.

questions.question: What kind of files does this lesson identify as historically used to save PyTorch weights, before safetensors?
options: Only .json files
`.bin` / `.pt` files, using Python's pickle format
Only .csv files
Only .safetensors files, from the very beginning
questions.explanation: The lesson identifies .bin and .pt files, based on Python's pickle format, as the format historically used to save PyTorch weights before safetensors became the safer standard.

lessons.title: Publishing a Model to the Hub
lessons.description: Push a fine-tuned model to the Hub so it can be loaded like any other repo.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe the steps to publish a fine-tuned model to the Hugging Face Hub.

sections.title: 📤 push_to_hub in one call
sections.content:
Both `Trainer` and PEFT models support `.push_to_hub(repo_id)`, which uploads the model weights, config, and tokenizer to a new or existing Hub repo — the same repo structure you learned to read in the very first lesson of this course, just from the publishing side now.

```python
trainer.push_to_hub("your-username/my-fine-tuned-model")
# or, for a PEFT/LoRA adapter:
peft_model.push_to_hub("your-username/my-lora-adapter")
```

sections.title: 📝 Writing your own model card
sections.content: Publishing without a model card leaves future users (including future you) without the training data, intended use, and limitations context that the earlier model-cards lesson taught you to look for in other people's models. Writing your own is the same discipline, applied to your own work.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Publishing without any model card at all.** Even a few sentences about training data and intended use is far better than nothing.

**Forgetting to set the repo's visibility intentionally.** Public vs. private matters for anything containing sensitive or proprietary training data.

**Publishing a model you haven't evaluated.** Push a model only after checking its metrics — publishing is a form of making a claim about what the model does.

questions.question: What does `trainer.push_to_hub(repo_id)` upload?
options: Only the training logs, nothing else
The model weights, config, and tokenizer to a new or existing Hub repo
Nothing — push_to_hub only validates the model without uploading
Only the dataset used for training
questions.explanation: push_to_hub bundles up everything needed to reload the model elsewhere — weights, config, and tokenizer — and uploads it to the specified Hub repo.

questions.question: Why should you write a model card when publishing your own fine-tuned model?
options: Model cards are purely optional decoration with no real use

It gives future users (including yourself later) the training data, intended use, and limitations context needed to use the model responsibly — the same information you learned to look for in others' models
Model cards are only required for datasets, not models
Writing a model card is required by the Hub's technical infrastructure to make the repo function
questions.explanation: The same information you check for in a model card when evaluating someone else's model (training data, intended use, limitations) is exactly what you owe to anyone who might later use a model you publish, including your future self.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to publish a model before evaluating it?
options: It's not a mistake — evaluation can always happen after publishing with no downside
Publishing effectively makes an implicit claim about what the model does, so publishing without evaluation risks sharing a model you haven't verified actually works as intended
Models cannot be evaluated once they're published
Evaluation is only relevant for very large models
questions.explanation: Once published, others may rely on your model's stated capabilities. Evaluating before publishing ensures the model actually does what you're implicitly claiming it does, rather than shipping unverified results.

questions.question: What does `trainer.push_to_hub(repo_id)` upload?
options: Only the training logs, nothing else
The model weights, config, and tokenizer to a new or existing Hub repo
Nothing — push_to_hub only validates the model without uploading anything
Only the dataset used for training
questions.explanation: push_to_hub bundles up everything needed to reload the model elsewhere — weights, config, and tokenizer — and uploads it to the specified Hub repo.

questions.question: Can a PEFT/LoRA model also be published with `push_to_hub`, according to this lesson?
options: No, push_to_hub only works for full Trainer-based models
Yes — peft_model.push_to_hub(repo_id) publishes a LoRA adapter the same way
PEFT models cannot be published to the Hub under any method
Only Trainer objects can ever call push_to_hub
questions.explanation: The lesson's example shows both trainer.push_to_hub() for a full model and peft_model.push_to_hub() for a LoRA adapter, confirming both can be published this way.

questions.question: Why should you write a model card when publishing your own fine-tuned model?
options: Model cards are purely optional decoration with no real use
It gives future users (including yourself later) the training data, intended use, and limitations context needed to use the model responsibly
Model cards are only required for datasets, never for models
Writing a model card is required by the Hub's technical infrastructure to function at all
questions.explanation: The same information you check for in a model card when evaluating someone else's model is exactly what you owe to anyone who might later use a model you publish, including your future self.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to publish a model before evaluating it?
options: It's not a mistake; evaluation can always happen after publishing with no downside
Publishing effectively makes an implicit claim about what the model does, so publishing without evaluation risks sharing an unverified model
Models cannot technically be evaluated once they're published
Evaluation is only relevant for very large models
questions.explanation: Once published, others may rely on your model's stated capabilities — evaluating before publishing ensures the model actually does what you're implicitly claiming it does.

questions.question: Why does the lesson emphasize setting a repo's visibility (public vs. private) intentionally when publishing?
options: Visibility settings have no real consequence for any repo
Visibility matters for anything containing sensitive or proprietary training data, so it shouldn't be left to a careless default
All repos are automatically private and cannot be changed
Only datasets have a visibility setting, not models
questions.explanation: The lesson warns against forgetting to set visibility intentionally, since public vs. private status matters significantly when a model involves sensitive or proprietary training data.

lessons.title: Licensing and Model Cards in Practice
lessons.description: Choose a license for your own model and write a model card that actually helps future users.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can choose an appropriate license for a model you publish and write a model card that covers the essentials.

sections.title: ⚖️ Picking a license for your own work
sections.content: When you publish, you choose the license — the same categories from the earlier lesson (permissive like Apache 2.0/MIT, or more restrictive) now apply to a decision you're making rather than one you're evaluating. Consider what training data you used: if it came with its own license restrictions, your fine-tuned model may inherit constraints from it.

sections.title: 📋 A minimal but real model card
sections.content:
At minimum, a useful model card states: what the model does, what data it was fine-tuned on, what metrics it achieves, and known limitations. This is the same checklist from the earlier model-cards lesson, just written from the author's side.

```markdown
## Model Card: sentiment-classifier-v1
- Base model: bert-base-uncased
- Fine-tuned on: IMDB movie reviews (50k examples)
- Metrics: 91% accuracy, 0.90 F1 on held-out test set
- Limitations: English only; may underperform on sarcasm and mixed-sentiment text
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Choosing a license without checking your training data's license.** If your training data has usage restrictions, your model may need to inherit them.

**Writing a model card with no metrics.** 'It works well' isn't a metric — report the actual numbers from your evaluation.

**Copying a generic model card template without customizing the limitations section.** Generic limitations don't help users who need to know about your specific model's actual failure modes.

questions.question: Why might the license of your training data affect the license you choose for your fine-tuned model?
options: Training data licenses never affect the resulting model's license
If the training data carries usage restrictions, the fine-tuned model may need to inherit or respect those same constraints
Only the base model's license matters, never the data's
Licensing only applies to code, never to trained models
questions.explanation: Just as understanding a model's license mattered when using someone else's model, the license terms attached to your training data can carry forward restrictions that affect how you're allowed to license and distribute your fine-tuned result.

questions.question: What should a minimal but genuinely useful model card include?
options: Nothing beyond the model's name
What the model does, what data it was fine-tuned on, what metrics it achieves, and known limitations
Only the file size of the model weights
A list of every hyperparameter tried during experimentation, with no summary
questions.explanation: These four elements — purpose, training data, metrics, and limitations — mirror the same checklist you learned to look for in others' model cards, giving future users the essentials to decide if the model fits their needs.

questions.question: Why is writing 'it works well' in a model card's metrics section insufficient?
options: It's actually a complete and sufficient description
It provides no concrete, comparable information — actual numbers (like accuracy or F1 on a specific test set) are what let someone judge the model's real performance
Model cards should never contain any numbers
Metrics sections are optional and can be left blank instead
questions.explanation: A vague claim gives no way to compare or verify performance. Concrete metrics — like a specific accuracy or F1 score on a stated test set — are what actually let a future user judge whether the model fits their needs.

questions.question: Why might the license of your training data affect the license you choose for your fine-tuned model?
options: Training data licenses never affect the resulting model's license
If the training data carries usage restrictions, the fine-tuned model may need to inherit or respect those same constraints
Only the base model's license matters, never the data's license
Licensing only applies to code, never to trained models
questions.explanation: Just as understanding a model's license mattered when using someone else's model, restrictions on your training data's license can carry forward and affect how you're allowed to license your fine-tuned result.

questions.question: What should a minimal but genuinely useful model card include, according to this lesson?
options: Nothing beyond the model's name
What the model does, what data it was fine-tuned on, what metrics it achieves, and known limitations
Only the file size of the model weights
A list of every hyperparameter tried, with no summary of results
questions.explanation: These four elements — purpose, training data, metrics, and limitations — mirror the same checklist you learned to look for in others' model cards.

questions.question: Why is writing 'it works well' in a model card's metrics section insufficient?
options: It's actually a complete and sufficient description of performance
It provides no concrete, comparable information — actual numbers like accuracy or F1 are what let someone judge real performance
Model cards should never contain any numbers at all
Metrics sections are entirely optional and can be left blank
questions.explanation: A vague claim gives no way to compare or verify performance; concrete metrics like a specific accuracy or F1 score on a stated test set are what actually let a future user judge whether the model fits their needs.

questions.question: What mistake does this lesson warn against regarding copying a generic model card template?
options: Using a template is always forbidden and should never be done
Copying a generic template without customizing the limitations section fails to convey the specific model's actual failure modes
Templates automatically fill in accurate limitations for every model
Only the metrics section ever needs customization, never the limitations
questions.explanation: Generic limitations copied from a template don't help users who need to know about the specific model's actual, particular failure modes rather than boilerplate text.

questions.question: What license categories does this lesson reference as applying to a decision you're now making as the model's author?
options: Only research-only licenses exist as an option
The same categories from the earlier lesson — permissive licenses like Apache 2.0/MIT, or more restrictive ones
Licensing categories only ever apply to datasets, never to models you publish
There is only a single universal license type for all models
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that the same license categories from the earlier model-cards lesson (permissive like Apache 2.0/MIT, or more restrictive) now apply to a decision you're actively making as the author, not just evaluating.

lessons.title: Spaces and Lightweight Deployment
lessons.description: Turn a model into a shareable demo without building a full backend from scratch.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe what a Hugging Face Space is and when it's a good fit for showing off a model.

sections.title: 🖥️ A demo app, hosted for you
sections.content:
A **Space** is a small hosted app (commonly built with Gradio or Streamlit) that runs alongside a model repo. It's the fastest way to give someone a working, in-browser demo of a model without building and hosting your own web server.

```python
# app.py for a simple Gradio Space
import gradio as gr
from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")

def predict(text):
    return classifier(text)[0]

gr.Interface(fn=predict, inputs="text", outputs="json").launch()
```

sections.title: 🚦 Demo vs. production, one more time
sections.content: A Space is perfect for showing a model works and letting people try it. It is not, by itself, a production-scale deployment — for real traffic, you'd move to a dedicated inference setup (covered in the inference and LLMOps tracks) with proper scaling, monitoring, and reliability guarantees.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating a Space as production infrastructure.** It's built for demos and light usage, not guaranteed uptime or high throughput.

**Loading a large model on a free-tier Space without checking hardware limits.** Free Spaces have limited compute; a large model may need a paid hardware tier or a smaller/quantized model.

**Forgetting to pin dependencies in the Space's requirements file.** An unpinned dependency update can silently break a working demo.

questions.question: What is a Hugging Face Space?
options: A place to store training data only
A small hosted app, commonly built with Gradio or Streamlit, that runs alongside a model repo to provide an in-browser demo
A type of model architecture
A production-grade load balancer
questions.explanation: A Space hosts a small interactive app — frequently a Gradio or Streamlit interface — letting anyone try a model in their browser without needing to set up their own server.

questions.question: Why shouldn't a Space typically be treated as production infrastructure?
options: Spaces are actually designed for and guarantee production-scale reliability
Spaces are built for demos and light usage, not guaranteed uptime, high throughput, or the scaling and monitoring a production deployment needs
Spaces cannot host any model at all
There is no difference between a Space and a production deployment
questions.explanation: A Space is optimized for quickly showing that something works, not for the reliability, scaling, and monitoring guarantees a real production system needs — that gap is exactly what dedicated inference and LLMOps setups are built to close.

questions.question: Why does pinning dependencies in a Space's requirements file matter?
options: It has no effect on whether the Space works
An unpinned dependency can update unexpectedly and silently break a previously working demo
Pinning dependencies is required by Hugging Face's terms of service only
Dependencies are automatically pinned and cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Without pinned versions, a library update could change behavior or break compatibility, causing a demo that worked yesterday to fail today with no code change on your part — pinning avoids this kind of silent breakage.

questions.question: Why does pinning dependencies in a Space's requirements file matter?
options: It has no effect on whether the Space works correctly

Dependencies are automatically pinned by default and cannot be changed

questions.question: What should you check before loading a large model on a free-tier Space, according to this lesson?
options: Nothing — free-tier Spaces have unlimited compute for any model size
The Space's hardware limits, since a large model may need a paid hardware tier or a smaller/quantized model
Only the model's license, never its hardware needs
Whether the model has ever been used in a Space before
questions.explanation: The lesson warns against loading a large model on a free-tier Space without checking hardware limits, since free Spaces have limited compute and may require a paid tier or a smaller/quantized model.
